6. He contends that in order to carry on the businesses of the petitioner-company, its subsidiaries and associates more economically, efficiently and conveniently as well as to improve and expand their current business position, it is necessary to avail credit facilities or amalgamate with or incorporate with any other company or companies having similar objects altogether or in part similar to those of this company and to gain the interest of the company altogether or in part, .the said amendments are necessary. He, then, submits that the application has been filed bonafide inasmuch as the said amendment would serve the interest of the members of the company and would not in any way adversely affect any creditor or other person or persons. Then, he takes me through the Memo No. SEC/ CMMRRCD/2006-159 /Admin/02-10 dated 26-11-2006 and, side-by-side, places before this Court the provisions of section 103 of the Companies Act and submits that there is no bar in law in giving guarantee to loans to be obtained by a company's subsidiary or holding or associate company while lending company has substantive share and holds directorship. He submits that since providing 'corporate guarantee' against the shareholding positions of the petitioner's company is a must in order to fulfill the requirements to the banking laws by the petitioner company, subsidiary or holding companies, therefore, the added provisions are required to be inserted in the MoA, otherwise the petitioner-company shall face difficulties/obstacles in conducting its business and, in elaborating this count of submission, he contends that since the petitioner-company has a subsidiary company, namely, Zodiac Power Chittagong Limited (ZPCL) and 5 (five) associate companies, namely, Confidence Electric Limited (CEL), Confidence Power Limited (CPL), Confidence Infrastructure Limited (CIL), Confidence Batteries Limited (CBL) and Confidence Power Holdings Limited (CPHL) and since their statements having been accepted are reflected in the annual report for the year ended 2019-2020 as per provisions of section 186 of Companies Act, therefore, for effective participation in the operations of those companies 'corporate guarantee' is obvious. 

 8. The learned Advocate for the respondent No. 2 (BSEC), Mr AM Masum, places the provisions of section 103(1) of the Companies Act and submits that the petitioner-company is not allowed to make any loan or give any guarantee or provide any security in connection with a loan made by a third party to any private company of which any director of the company is a director or member, and although some exceptions are provided in the said law but the petitioner company's scenario is not covered by the said exceptions. Mr AM Masum, thereafter, refers to section 121 (1) of the Companies Act and submits that the petitioner-company is also debarred under section 121(1) of the Companies Act from adding the clauses in question in MoA, as the petitioner-company is not the Managing Agent of the companies for whom the proposed clauses are going to be added. 

 10. When the hearing of this case was going on, Mr Imtiaz Farooq, an Advocate of this Court, expressed his willingness to make some arguments on the issues involved in this case. This Court, then, allowed Mr Imtiaz Farooq to make his submissions as an Amicus Curie. Thereafter, he presented a very useful written skeleton submission before this Court. The substance of his opinion is that in light of section 103 of the Companies Act, a listed public company can provide guarantee or security to secure loans given to its subsidiaries only (i.e., where the listed company holds more than 50% share of the borrower company) to the extent of its shareholding (and not to associate companies or third parties), subject to satisfying the additional conditions regarding approval procedure in the Board and general meeting as well as making explicit reference in its balance sheet; that unlike in India, to satisfy section 103, the subsidiary does not have to be wholly owned subsidiary, merely fulfilling the conditions of subsidiary under section 2 of the Companies Act shall suffice, subject to the condition that the guarantee/security provided cannot be more than the shareholding of the guarantor company in the borrower company. 

 34. Although with the above conclusion, the issue No. 4, namely, whether a listed company can stand as a surety or guarantor of a private company, has become redundant, nonetheless, I will take up the issue for examination for an effective disposal of this case. And, for the said purpose, section 103 of the Companies Act may now be quoted herein below: 

 103. Loan of Director:- (1) No company, hereinafter in this section referred to as the lending company, shall make any loan or give any guarantee or provide any security in connection with a loan made by a third party to— 

 35. From a minute reading of section 103 of the Companies Act, it appears to me that it provides a safety mechanism for protecting the shareholders of the guarantor company by prohibiting,  amongst others, providing guarantee or mortgage by a company (guarantor company) to secure loans given by third parties to another company (borrower company) where: (i) in case of borrower company being a private company the guarantor company and borrower company has common shareholder(s)/director(s); (ii) in case of borrower company being a public company the borrower company is run as per directions of the guarantor company. The intent of this prohibition under section 103 of the Companies Act is to ensure that directors do not surpass their fiduciary duty towards the guarantor company for personal benefit and section 103 provides exemption from such prohibition if all of the following three conditions satisfy: (a) guarantor company is a banking company, or the guarantor company is a private company which is not a subsidiary of a public company, or the guarantor company as a holding company makes the loan or gives the guarantee or provide the security to its subsidiary, (b) the guarantee/security is sanctioned by the Board of Directors of guarantor company and approved by the general meeting and, in the balance sheet, there is a specific mention of the loan, guarantee or security as the case may be and (c) in case where the guarantor company is the holding company of the borrower company, the amount of guarantee does not exceed the shareholding of the guarantor company in the borrower company. 

 36. The combined reading of restrictions and exceptions in section 103 of the Companies Act mean that in a case, as in the instant petition, where a listed public company as guarantor company wishes to provide guarantee or security for loans given to another company, only scope for providing such guarantee/security would be in case of securing loans granted to its subsidiary to the extent of its shareholding. The restrictions under section 103 of the Companies Act have also been specially made mandatory for a listed company, like the instant petitioner company, by an Order dated 10-9-2006 by the BSEC and the intention of the Legislature is clear, that where the shareholders of the company, being the ultimate owners, themselves approve the utilization of the funds of the public company for its subsidiaries, the law need not create a bar to the same. Thus, the general prohibition is exempted to an extent by providing for a way out in the form of a shareholders' resolution for granting of loans/guarantees/securities to subsidiaries only so that shareholders are not prejudiced. However, any breach of section 103 of the Companies Act would, amongst others, result in cessation of directors of the guarantor public company who are also directors of the borrower private company, as stipulated in section 108(1)(g) of the Companies Act. Since nowadays a tendency prevails among the promoters of the listed entities to source funds through various complex structures and structured obligations, for which the listed companies are providing corporate guarantees, though it may be risky and detrimental to the interest of their shareholders, therefore, in order to protect the interests of shareholders, a listed entity must obtain prior approval from the public/general shareholders before extending any loan, guarantee or security for the benefit of the promoters' other entities. 

 38. Therefore, the instant application may be allowed to the extent of providing guarantee or security for loans extended to subsidiaries only and subject to the procedural safeguards provided in section 103 of the Companies Act and BSEC Order dated 10-9-2006 or as the law may prescribe from time to time.
